proof.surface: The real cmd/broker binary built from this head, started by hand on a real Postgres 17.11 of its own, once per store a pod can mount, driven with curl from one source address through BROKER_TRUSTED_PROXY_HEADER until that address's own bucket refuses. Retry-After is the observable: it carries the refusing bucket's own Every, so it says which bucket refused and at what rate.
proof.command: go build -o $TMPDIR/hand/broker ./cmd/broker; then bash $TMPDIR/hand/peraddr.sh, which drives POST /v1/secrets/AUTO_READ_TOKEN/reread from 203.0.113.7 past the shared bucket's own refusals on an aws-secrets-manager broker and then on a gcp-secret-manager one
proof.observed: aws-secrets-manager (shared Every 1s): 49 accepted from the one address, the shared bucket refusing 83 times with Retry-After: 1 along the way, and then that address's OWN bucket refused with **Retry-After: 2** — twice the bucket this process mounts, and exactly the figure the route had before this issue. gcp-secret-manager (shared Every 4s): 49 accepted, the shared bucket refusing 344 times with Retry-After: 4, then the address's own bucket with **Retry-After: 8**. The same ordering on both stores, each derived from its own mount. At the previous head the AWS case gave Retry-After: 8 against a shared 1. api.DefaultRereadLimit is gone from the tree: `grep -rn DefaultRereadLimit packages/envoy docs` finds nothing, in code or in documentation.
proof.negativeControl: Two, each isolating one half. (a) A go build overlay replacing only `reread := RereadLimitFor(rereadOverall)` in Register with the old constant, the repository untouched: my behavioural row goes red with 'one address's own reread bucket refuses with Retry-After "8" against a shared bucket refilling every 1s; want "2"'. (b) An overlay setting perAddressFactor to 1 and nothing else: the implementer's own safety row goes red on both mounts ('gives one address one every 1s; want at least 2s', and the same for 4s/8s). So the behavioural row proves Register mounts the derivation and the unit row proves the derivation's output is safe, and each fails when its own half is removed.

proof.criterion: The new oauthSecretTimeout headroom row measures what it says it measures, and its stated cause for the figure is right.
proof.surface: The row itself against a real Postgres, and the same row under overlays that warm the pool before the race, so that the connection open and the row-lock contention can be told apart.
proof.command: go test -run TestOAuthProviderSecretUnderATwoPodBootIsFarInsideItsTimeout ./cmd/broker, then the same under an overlay adding one warm-up Secret call, then under one adding two concurrent warm-up calls
proof.observed: At the head: 12.2 ms and 3.6 ms against the 10 s bound, inside the quarter-bound margin by a factor of 200. The row's stated cause — 'each goroutine's first call also opens its pooled connection' — is right, and I isolated it: with ONE warm-up call the faster side drops to 0.8-1.5 ms while the slower stays 14-17 ms (the pool still has to open a second connection); with TWO concurrent warm-up calls, so both pooled connections already exist, both sides are 0.7-1.6 ms over four runs. So the whole of the double-digit figure is connection setup and the contention the bound exists for is sub-millisecond, which agrees with the 2.7-6.3 ms psql measurement the constant's comment carries with its own caveat.
proof.negativeControl: The three measurements are the control for each other: the only difference between them is how many pooled connections exist when the race starts, and the figure falls from 12-17 ms to under 2 ms as that goes from none to two. The row asserts a margin (a quarter of the bound) rather than a duration, so it goes red only if that margin collapses by two orders of magnitude.
